ValidYN="Y">10.1016/j.ibneur.2026.03.003</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText Label="BACKGROUND" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) reflects neuronal degeneration and is likely a disease-progression biomarker in Parkinson's disease (PD). Therapies shown to decrease serum NfL in PD may provide disease-modifying effects. Serum glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) may predict more rapid cognitive decline in PD.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Serum samples from two PD trials were assessed for NfL and GFAP using the SIMOA platform at baseline and after 24-weeks of lithium therapy. Post hoc, patients were divided into three groups defined by their serum lithium levels at week 24: "high lithium" (0.21-0.56 mmol/L, median=0.32 mmol/L, <i>n</i> = 10), "medium lithium" (0.14-0.20 mmol/L, median=0.17 mmol/L, <i>n</i> = 8) and "low lithium" (<0.10-0.12 mmol/L, median<0.10 mmol/L, <i>n</i> = 10). Pairwise comparisons were performed using the Fisher-Pitman permutation test.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">Median % 24-week changes in serum NfL were -12.8, -2.0 and 11.2 in the high, medium and low lithium groups, respectively. Pairwise group comparisons showed significant differences between high and low lithium (<i>p</i> = 0.0001) and high and medium lithium (<i>p</i> = 0.0203) but not medium and low lithium groups (<i>p</i> = 0.0907). Median % 24-week changes in serum GFAP were 7.3, 42.8 and 12.4, respectively. Pairwise comparisons showed a significant difference between the high and medium lithium (<i>p</i> = 0.0075) but not the high and low lithium (<i>p</i> = 0.1763) or medium and low lithium groups (<i>p</i> = 0.3950).</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">In this post hoc analysis from two small clinical trials, lithium aspartate therapy achieving a median serum lithium level of 0.32 mmol/L was associated with a significant reduction in serum NfL in PD. Because serum NfL is likely a disease-progression biomarker in PD, further clinical investigation of lithium's effects on serum NfL and potential disease-modifying effects in PD is merited.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="UNASSIGNED">"High lithium" therapy, achieving a median serum level of 0.32 mmol/L, was associated with a significant reduction in serum NfL in PD. Although wogonin has demonstrated efficacy against oxidative stress and inflammation, its mechanistic role in Parkinson's disease (PD) remains incompletely understood. The present study investigated the neuroprotective potential of wogonin in a rotenone-induced mice model of PD, with particular emphasis on modulation of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β), a key kinase implicated in dopaminergic neurodegeneration. Swiss albino mice (n = 30) were randomly divided into five groups (six animals each): normal control (0.9% NaCl), rotenone (2 mg/kg, i.p.), wogonin (10 mg/kg, i.p.), wogonin (20 mg/kg, i.p.), and lithium chloride (LiCl; 300 mg/kg, p.o.). Treatments were administered for 21 days. Behavioral assessments, including rotarod, open field, string and narrow beam walk tests were conducted on days 0, 7, 14, and 21. On day 22nd, animals were sacrificed for biochemical, neuroinflammatory and neurotransmitter analysis. Wogonin treatment significantly improved motor coordination, balance and grip strength compared with rotenone treated mice. Biochemical analysis revealed reduced malondialdehyde and nitrite levels along with increased glutathione levels in wogonin treated groups. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay demonstrated significant reductions in interleukin-6, caspase-3 and GSK-3β levels accompanied by restoration of striatal dopamine content. In conclusion, wogonin attenuated motor dysfunction, oxidative stress and neuroinflammation in a rotenone induced PD model through inhibition of GSK-3β signaling, highlighting its therapeutic potential against PD.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026 International Brain Research Organization (IBRO).
